title: Generalized Jacobians
summary: Generalized Jacobians include ordinary Jacobians as the zero-modulus case. The library constructs them over arbitrary fields and proves modulus existence and unique factorization for maps from open curves to commutative algebraic groups, with further results on conductors and étale cohomology.
overview: A generalized Jacobian associates an algebraic group to a smooth proper curve and an effective divisor, called a modulus. For the zero modulus it recovers the ordinary Jacobian, which represents degree-zero line bundles. The library constructs these groups over arbitrary fields, proves the zero-modulus comparison as an isomorphism of group schemes, and proves compatibility with field extensions.

The modulus extends Abel–Jacobi factorization to maps from open curves into commutative algebraic groups. For a map to a separated commutative group scheme locally of finite type, the library constructs a full Cartier modulus over the original field and proves unique equivariant factorization through its Picard degree-one torsor. A rational point sent to the identity gives a unique group homomorphism from the generalized Jacobian. Over an algebraically closed field, a regular map has a least full conductor; the conductor of a product map is the coefficientwise maximum of those of its components.

For ordinary Jacobians, the library constructs the Abel–Jacobi map and proves its pointed factorization property for maps to abelian varieties. Over algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero, the selected cohomology results measure genus and the contribution of punctures.
scopeNote: The generalized-Jacobian factorization is over arbitrary fields and constructs its modulus from the original map; uniqueness concerns the factor pair for the returned modulus. The conductor theorem uses an algebraically closed field. The cohomology formulas assume characteristic zero.

entries.title: Generalized Jacobians: existence of a modulus and unique factorization
entries.summary: Every map from a nonempty open curve to a separated commutative group locally of finite type constructs a full modulus and a unique equivariant Picard-one factorization over its original field.
statement: Let $k$ be any field, let $C/k$ be a smooth proper geometrically integral curve, let $U\subseteq C$ be a nonempty open subscheme, and let $G/k$ be a separated commutative group scheme locally of finite type. Given a $k$-morphism $q:U\to G$, there is a full effective Cartier divisor $D$ over $k$ with $C\setminus|D|=U$ for which $q$ satisfies the geometric modulus condition.

For this returned divisor, let $J_D$ be the generalized Jacobian, $J_D^1$ its intrinsic Picard-one torsor, and $a_D^1:U\to J_D^1$ the Abel map. There is a unique pair consisting of a group-scheme morphism $\phi:J_D\to G$ and a $k$-morphism $F:J_D^1\to G$ such that
where equivariance holds on points valued in every $k$-scheme. For the resulting modulus $D$, the pair $(\phi,F)$ is unique.

If a point $\varepsilon\in U(k)$ is supplied and $q(\varepsilon)=1$, there is also a direct pointed form: the map constructs such a divisor $D$ and a unique group-scheme morphism $\phi:J_D\to G$ with $q=\phi\circ a_{D,\varepsilon}$. Two maps from the same $U$ can be given a common ground-field modulus.
discussion: A modulus retains boundary multiplicities and controls maps to commutative algebraic groups. The theorem factors the given morphism through the Picard degree-one torsor of a suitable modulus.

Serre develops maps from curves to commutative groups and generalized Jacobians in Chapters III and V of Algebraic Groups and Class Fields. The formal result links modulus existence to the constructed group and torsor over the original field, while keeping the full Cartier divisor and the equivariance equation.
history: The modulus approach connects the mapping properties of open curves with generalized Jacobians. Chapters III and V of Serre's Algebraic Groups and Class Fields provide the mathematical reference for these two parts.

entries.title: Pointed maps from curves to abelian varieties factor uniquely through Abel–Jacobi
entries.summary: Every pointed morphism from the curve to an abelian variety factors uniquely through the fixed Jacobian.
statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $C/k$ be smooth, proper, geometrically irreducible, and of relative dimension $1$, and choose $P\in C(k)$. Let $A/k$ be a smooth proper geometrically irreducible group scheme. For a $k$-morphism $f:C\to A$ with $f(P)=0$,
The quantified $g$ in the cited declaration is a morphism in the category of schemes over $k$.
discussion: This universal property reduces the study of pointed maps from the curve to the study of maps out of its Jacobian. Sending the base point to zero removes translation freedom, and uniqueness makes the factorization a characterization of the Jacobian. It is the curve case of the Albanese viewpoint, which characterizes a variety through its maps to abelian varieties; Milne develops it in Section 6.
history: The Albanese viewpoint characterizes a variety by its maps to abelian varieties. For a pointed curve, its Jacobian has this universal role. Milne treats this characterization in Section 6, alongside the duality theory of Jacobians.

entries.title: Least conductors exist, and the conductor of a product map is their coefficientwise maximum
entries.summary: An actual map from an open curve constructs its unique least full conductor, with an exact coefficientwise formula for product-valued maps.
statement: Let $k$ be algebraically closed in any characteristic, let $C/k$ be a smooth proper integral curve, let $U\subseteq C$ be nonempty, and let $q:U\to G$ be a morphism to a separated commutative group scheme locally of finite type. Let $a_q$ be its function on places with values in $G(k)$, equal to the actual point values on $U$ and extended by the identity outside $U$. In additive notation, having full modulus $E$ means $\sum_v\operatorname{ord}_v(f)a_q(v)=0$ for every nonzero rational function $f\equiv1\pmod E$. Thus the conductor here classifies moduli of the specified point-value function on all places.

The inequality compares every place multiplicity. The conductor has coefficient zero at all places centered in $U$; its support may be strictly smaller than $C\setminus U$. The map admits a modulus and a unique reciprocal local symbol.

discussion: A modulus can often be enlarged, so existence alone leaves many choices. The conductor removes that ambiguity by specifying the least allowed multiplicity at every place. Classifying all moduli as those above it is stronger than finding a modulus of minimum total degree.

For a map to a product group, each coordinate imposes its own condition and the least simultaneous bound is their coefficientwise maximum. The calculation uses the actual regular maps and applies to nonproper targets as well. The local-symbol and modulus viewpoint is developed in Serre’s Algebraic Groups and Class Fields.
history: Serre’s treatment of maps from curves to commutative algebraic groups uses moduli and local symbols to describe their boundary behavior and their relation to generalized Jacobians.

discussion: Kummer theory and Jacobian torsion connect the genus with finite abelian covering data. For an open curve, the boundary contributes r−1 additional directions. The two formulas are presented together, with their respective hypotheses.
history: SGA 1 established the fundamental-group language for finite étale covers. In the Jacobian setting, the relation between abelian covers and torsion is developed in Milne's Jacobian Varieties, Section 9; Kummer theory provides the cohomological expression used here.

The classical theory of generalized Jacobians incorporates boundary conditions into the geometry of divisor classes. Milne's Sections 8–9 place punctured-curve covering questions in this broader setting. The formula here expresses the boundary contribution through étale cohomology.
